body: Adrian from Toronto, Canada asks in a callout question: How do I make my fridge work better? In my mini fridge, cans sometimes get so cold that they explode, and sometimes milk goes bad faster. Is uneven refrigeration something I can improve, or is it just a sign of a bad fridge?

Rachel: My first thought here is to make sure your refrigerator is not overfilled. Uneven refrigeration could be due to lack of airflow if you have too much on your shelves. If this is not the case, it would be best to call in a professional. It could be something like a poor seal or an issue with the coils.
This is a little out of my expertise so I would definitely get someone in to take a look at it.

articles.title: Sin or virtue? How envy can actually be helpful
articles.summary: In her new book, Envy, Stacy Kim explains how to understand the feeling, identify your deeper desires and use them to achieve your goals. In the 16th-century poem The Faerie Queene, envy is a ghoulish figure riding a ravenous wolf, sad to see the fortune of others and “wonderous glad” of their…
body: Maybe not. “I think that when we don’t examine our envy, that’s when it leads us astray,” says Dr Stacy Kim, social scientist, life coach and author of the new book Envy: Why Wanting What They Have is the Key to Getting What You Want. Kim wrote the book after seeing the way envy came up for her coaching clients and reflecting on the role it had in her own life. The book is informed by social science and philosophy research, as well as her personal and professional experiences.

To Kim, a lifelong envier who says sibling rivalry propelled her to fast-track a PhD in educational policy and leadership, envy tells you “there’s something important here,” Kim says. “Envy signals to us our goals,” as well as “what is within our reach”, as we tend to envy people similar to ourselves more so than, say, superstars.
But how to transform envy from sulky to superpower? Kim gave us some points to consider.
Envy is “simply wanting something that someone else has”, Kim says. “Everyone envies – it’s normal.”

articles.title: Inside the New D.C. Restaurant That Only Sells Five Curry Steak Frites Every Night
articles.summary: The hottest new spot in Washington, D.C. focuses on the traditional heat-packed cooking methods of northern Thailand, while still using local ingredients from around the DMV.
body: Elsewhere in the kitchen, another chef carves green papayas. The irregular slices of papaya get tossed in a funky, spicy dressing for each order. Ko calls it the “most labor intensive dish on the line;” each order is carefully mixed with fresh tomatoes, peanuts, and a palm syrup and tamarind-heavy dressing. A rich pork belly curry is simmering in the background. Gaeng hung lay (a traditional northern Thai curry) cooks down large pieces of pork belly to get that fatty layer, with pickled garlic and pineapple balancing out the rich flavors of curry paste, tamarind, and fish sauce.

Right before service, the chefs begin prepping herbs and sticky rice that has been soaking overnight and is quickly steamed for that malleable, glutinous texture. McCoy talks about how being a chef is more of a lifestyle than a job, but there’s immense payoff when you get to see diners enjoy your hard work every night. He hopes that Alfie’s will become a place where “you can just forget where you are, have a good time, and just lose yourself in the experience and the food.”
Watch the kitchen team at Aflie’s cook classic Thai dishes and fusion plates like curry steak frites in this episode of Now Open.

articles.title: A job that changed me: I was a rookie tour guide for art lovers – no one goes harder than active seniors in search of cultural enrichment
articles.summary: I spent time in some of the greatest art institutions with groups of self-funded retirees. But a vacation it was not. In 2012 I was living in Sydney, halfway through the shelf life of our annual theatric political satire The Wharf Revue, although I didn’t know that at the time.
body: Handling the art side of things was my gallery colleague Brian Ladd and together we landed in a wintry Manhattan in January with about 25 guests largely, shall we say, a certain demographic who were keen to sample the cultural delights of the great metropolis.

And let’s face it, there’s no shortage of them. We took in the Metropolitan Museum and the Cloisters, MoMA, the Frick, the Whitney, Radio City, the Brooklyn Museum, the Guggenheim, the High Line, half a dozen shows and several exhaustive bus tours from one end of the island to the other with our indefatigable local guide Frederique. We even managed a backstage tour of the Met, led by a volunteer who actually paid for the privilege of conducting them! A full-on schedule but, let me tell you, no one goes harder than an active senior in search of cultural enrichment. By the end of the 10 days, we were desperately in need of a holiday.

body: These days, you can’t scroll, shop, or even walk down the street without hearing about peptides. And while they’re in everything from supplements to IVs, the best peptide serums stand apart for their ability to boost hydration, increase collagen and elastin, and deliver smoother, more youthful skin—with the evidence to back up many of their claims.

But even in skincare, these ingredients are enjoying newfound attention. “ Peptides have graduated from the fine print to the front of the bottle,” says Mona Gohara, MD, a board-certified dermatologist in Hamden, Connecticut. They’re quickly approaching hyaluronic acid -territory—which itself has become a household name—in part due to their versatility. “Many peptide formulas offer improvements in the appearance of fine lines and firmness while being relatively easy to tolerate and incorporate into a routine,” she says. “They also pair beautifully with ingredients such as hyaluronic acid, niacinamide, and antioxidants.”

articles.title: Is Your ‘Organic’ Skin Care Actually Organic?
articles.summary: In 2026, organic skin care refers to how ingredients are sourced, grown, and processed, but does that make them automatically better? Here, Vogue unpacks what to look for in organic skin-care products and the best products to shop.
body: Organic; clean; 100% natural. The labels certainly blur together fast. And if you’ve ever shopped for a beauty product, you, like me, may have been puzzled by trying to understand them. In 2026, while consumer desire for transparency and sustainability is at an all-time high, the organic skin-care search is striking a particular intrigue.

“In the early years, organic felt like a discovery, a reason to look more closely at what we were putting on our skin,” says aesthetician and founder of Monastery, Athena Hewett. “Today, it’s an invitation to look at a product a bit more closely. How was it extracted? What is it actually doing in the formula? Organic is meaningful, but it doesn’t tell the entire story of a product.”

articles.title: The Locals' Guide to the Mexico City Grand Prix Weekend
articles.summary: In Mexico City, the energy of race weekend spills beyond the track and into the city.
body: Enrique del Bosque has attended his fair share of Formula 1 races around the world. From iconic circuits like the Autodromo Nazionale Monza in Italy —the famed home of Team Ferrari—to newer racetracks in Las Vegas and Lusail City in Qatar, the Mexican content creator with the largest F1-related TikTok following in Latin America has been a guest at plenty of paddocks and VIP parties.
Still, he says, nothing compares to the festive spirit that accompanies the Mexico City Grand Prix.

“Other [destinations] are mostly about the racing,” del Bosque says. “Mexico has its own flavor. The party is bigger, especially with important cultural events like Día de Muertos going on at the same time.” He also references chilango—a term used for Mexico City residents and their bombastic, out-of-pocket antics—that gives the city a uniquely local sporting energy.

articles.title: Here are 10 Full-Sized Liquid Items That You Can Actually Carry On Board a Flight
articles.summary: Among the items that are allowed above the limit are contact lens solution, baby food, and even live fish in water.
body: For years, travelers have become accustomed to meticulously packing liquids ranging from shampoo to sunscreen in their carry-on bags in order to meet the TSA liquid limit—and avoid getting that expensive perfume confiscated.

While commonly referred to as “liquids,” these regulated substances are technically known as LAGs, an abbreviation for liquids, aerosols, and gels. This category also encompasses creams or pastes—essentially anything that can be cut through or spread with a butter knife—from common travel necessities like shampoo, face wash, and sunscreen, to toothpaste, hairspray, and even peanut butter.

The Transportation Security Administration (TSA) first introduced the rule in August 2006, after British police foiled a terrorist plot to detonate explosive liquid in soda cans on flights from London to the US and Canada—prompting countries around the world to adopt the new airport security measure.
